comments.body:
CRITERION: "state whether the two 2026-07-30 lease losses were genuine takeovers or spurious classifications — or, if no new occurrence has been captured, say so explicitly rather than closing on inference."

STATEMENT: **They cannot be classified, and no new occurrence has been captured.** Not
"probably spurious", not "probably genuine" — unknown, and unknowable from what exists.

The two events are Reconcile Bridge runs 30576272914 (2026-07-30T19:52Z) and
30579382013 (20:38Z), both aborting with:

    ref-lock renew: refs/reconciler/lock CAS rejected — lease lost/stolen
    ERROR: reconcile heartbeat lost the lease (pass_id=...) — aborting pass

Why they cannot be resolved retroactively: the branch that made the "lease
lost/stolen" claim raised WITHOUT logging the git stderr that justified it. The
evidence that would distinguish a genuine `stale info` lease mismatch from one of the
non-lease rejections this ticket fixed was discarded at the moment of the claim. It is
gone; no amount of re-reading the logs recovers it.

Circumstantial signals exist and are deliberately NOT being treated as an answer:
  * both landed ~86s into the pass, on the SECOND heartbeat tick (lease 120s,
    interval 40s) — an oddly precise coincidence for two independent events;
  * `renew`'s pre-CAS `read()` force-fetches from origin and saw the ref still at our
    own oid immediately before the push CAS failed;
  * no other run in the window logged a steal, and the workflow's
    `concurrency: reconcile-bridge` group serialises passes.
Those lean toward spurious. They are not proof, and this ticket does not claim they
are. Recording the lean explicitly so a future investigator has the thread without
mistaking it for a conclusion.

What this ticket's fix actually buys: the NEXT occurrence is diagnosable. The CAS
branch now logs the stderr, so the same question asked again will have an answer.

This criterion therefore closes as "explicitly stated, unresolved" — which is the
disposition the criterion itself names as acceptable ("or, if no new occurrence has
been captured, say so explicitly"). It does NOT close as resolved. If a lease loss
recurs with the new logging in place, the classification should be recorded here or on
a follow-up rather than the question being dropped.

## Summary

`_PUSH_REJECT_MARKERS` in `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/_ref_lock.py:723`
over-matches, so several push failures that are **not** compare-and-swap mismatches
are classified as one — which the ref-lock reports as "lease lost/stolen". The same
branch discards the git stderr, so a production occurrence cannot be diagnosed after
the fact.

Found while root-causing bug `449f-f9bf-be90-47fe`. Filed separately because fixing
it changes lock classification semantics, and (see below) the very logging gap it
creates is why we cannot yet prove it has fired in production.

## The code

```python
# A rejected ``--force-with-lease`` prints "stale info" (the lease mismatch) or a
# "! [rejected]" / "cannot lock ref" line — distinct from a genuine transport
# failure ("Authentication failed", "Could not resolve host"), which we do NOT
# classify as a CAS mismatch (fail-closed).
_PUSH_REJECT_MARKERS = ("stale info", "rejected", "cannot lock ref")
```

`_push_lease_cas` (`:726-747`) lowercases stderr, substring-matches those markers,
and on a hit raises a synthetic `CalledProcessError(128, ["git","update-ref",ref])`
that `_cas_once` reads as a CAS mismatch and `renew` (`:570-572`) converts to
`LeaseLostError` -> heartbeat abort -> pass abort.

## Evidence — runtime, driving `_push_lease_cas` with real git stderr strings

```
genuine CAS mismatch (stale info)              CLASSIFIED AS CAS MISMATCH   <- correct
server-side concurrent ref lock (NOT CAS)      CLASSIFIED AS CAS MISMATCH   <- wrong
remote internal rejection (NOT CAS)            CLASSIFIED AS CAS MISMATCH   <- wrong
pre-receive hook declined (NOT CAS)            CLASSIFIED AS CAS MISMATCH   <- wrong
GitHub secondary rate limit (NOT CAS)          CLASSIFIED AS CAS MISMATCH   <- wrong
transport: auth failed                         fail-closed                  <- correct
transport: host unresolved                     fail-closed                  <- correct
```

The strings used are real git output shapes, e.g.
`error: cannot lock ref 'refs/reconciler/lock': Unable to create '...lock': File exists.`
and `! [remote rejected] refs/reconciler/lock (pre-receive hook declined)`.

`"rejected"` in particular matches `! [remote rejected]`, which git emits for hook
declines, quota/rate-limit rejections, and server-side errors — none of which mean
the lease moved.

## The contract this violates

The module's own comment at `_ref_lock.py:719-722` promises the opposite: a genuine
transport failure "we do NOT classify as a CAS mismatch (fail-closed)". ADR 0031
(`docs/adr/0031-reconciler-ref-lock.md:66,92`) states the same in its "Three exit-128
outcomes, one classifier" section. ADR 0031:189-190 additionally asserts "a **live**
holder is never stolen (regression-tested)".

## The compounding defect — the evidence is thrown away

The classified branch (`:743-745`) raises **without logging**. The fail-closed branch
below it (`:746-752`) *does* log the stderr. So the one path that makes a
consequential claim ("your lease was stolen") is the one that keeps no evidence for
it.

Concrete cost: `Reconcile Bridge` runs 30576272914 and 30579382013 (2026-07-30)
aborted on `LeaseLostError`. Both landed ~86s into the pass, on the **second**
heartbeat tick (lease 120s, interval 40s), and `renew`'s pre-CAS `read()` — which
force-fetches from origin — saw the ref still at our own oid immediately before the
push CAS failed. No other run logged a steal, and the workflow's
`concurrency: reconcile-bridge` group serializes passes. That pattern is suspicious
but **unprovable either way**, because the stderr that would settle it was discarded.

## Why this is filed, not fixed inline

Narrowing the markers changes what the lock treats as contention versus fault, on
`acquire` / `release` / `renew` / `steal` alike. That is a real blast radius, and the
occurrence rate is currently unmeasurable. The right order is: restore the evidence
first, then narrow once a real sample exists.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The CAS-mismatch branch logs the git stderr (and the ref + expected oid) before
      raising, at a level that survives into CI logs — so the next occurrence is
      diagnosable. This alone is low-risk and should land first.
- [ ] On `LeaseLostError`, the holder additionally records what the remote ref
      actually was (e.g. an `ls-remote` of the lock ref plus the holder recorded in
      the lock blob), so "stolen by whom" is answerable rather than inferred.
- [ ] The marker set no longer classifies non-CAS rejections (hook decline, server
      ref-lock contention, rate limit, internal error) as a lease mismatch, with a
      unit test driving the real stderr shapes above and asserting the split. RED
      first against the current list.
- [ ] Fail-closed behaviour for genuine transport failures (auth, DNS) is unchanged
      and still covered.
- [ ] With the logging in place, state whether the two 2026-07-30 lease losses were
      genuine takeovers or spurious classifications — or, if no new occurrence has
      been captured, say so explicitly rather than closing on inference.
- [ ] File paths: `src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/_ref_lock.py` (lines 715-752,
      and the `renew`/`LeaseLostError` path around 559-601).
compiled_state.title: _PUSH_REJECT_MARKERS misclassifies non-CAS push failures as a stolen lease, and discards the stderr that would prove it
